passages.t: A young king seeks God and cleanses the land
passages.happening:
‘Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years’ (verse 1). ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left’ (verse 2). ‘In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David, and in the twelfth year he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images’ (verse 3). The altars of the Baals are torn down, and the purge reaches the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim and Simeon, as far as Naphtali (verses 4-7).

In his eighteenth year he sends officials to repair the house of the LORD. The money gathered by the Levites from all Israel and Judah is paid to the workmen, who work faithfully under Levite overseers, some of them skilled musicians (verses 8-13).
passages.hearers:
Manasseh's long reign and Amon's short one left Judah soaked in idols. Josiah is the last great reforming king of David's line, and his reform has two stages: a young king's own seeking of God and his cleansing of the land, then the finding of the law, which deepens everything. Readers who know the ending feel the poignancy: this is the last bright light before the dark.

Josiah reigned about 640 to 609 BC. The years in verses 3 and 8 place his seeking of God around 632 BC, the start of his purge around 628 BC, and the finding of the book in his eighteenth year, commonly dated 622 BC. These were the decades of Assyria's collapse. After Ashurbanipal's death around 631 BC the empire weakened quickly, and Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. That vacuum may explain how Josiah could carry his reform into the old northern lands. Jeremiah and Zephaniah spoke in his reign.

Second Kings places the whole purge after the finding of the book; Chronicles begins it earlier and makes the book the climax. Burning the bones of priests on their altars defiled those altars for good, so they could not be used again.
passages.later: Jeremiah dates his call to this reign: ‘The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah’ (Jeremiah 1:2).
passages.asks: Josiah began to seek God while he was still young, before anyone had found the book. Ask what you know of God now that you could act on before you know more. And ask whether there is a young person near you whose seeking you could encourage.

passages.t: The book is found, and the king tears his clothes
passages.happening:
‘While they were bringing out the money that had been taken into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD written by Moses’ (verse 14). He says to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” (verse 15). Shaphan reports on the money and then reads the book to the king (verses 16-18). ‘When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes’ (verse 19). He sends to inquire of the LORD, ‘For great is the wrath of the LORD that has been poured out on us because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD’ (verse 21).

They go to Huldah the prophetess. She says that disaster will come on this place, as the book says, but to the king: ‘because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard His words against this place and against its people’ (verse 27), ‘Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place and on its inhabitants’ (verse 28). The king gathers all the people, reads the whole book to them, and makes a covenant before the LORD by the pillar (verses 29-31). ‘Throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Scrolls could easily be lost in a temple full of storerooms, especially after decades of neglect. The discovery is told with understatement: Shaphan reports the money first and only then mentions the book. The word book, sefer, comes ten times. Tearing one's clothes was a public act of grief or horror, the natural response to hearing the covenant's curses and knowing they applied.

Huldah, a prophetess living in the Second District, probably a newer quarter of Jerusalem, is consulted even though Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active, and nothing treats this as unusual; her word is received as the LORD's. Her oracle has two parts, one for this place and one for the king, separating judgment on the nation from mercy to the man. Tender, rakhakh, means soft and responsive; humbled, kana, links Josiah with Manasseh and with 7:14. Covenant renewals, a leader reading the law aloud and the people pledging to keep it, had precedents at Sinai, at Shechem under Joshua, and under Jehoiada.
passages.later: At Sinai, Moses ‘took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people’ (Exodus 24:7), and they answered, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exodus 24:7).
passages.hard:
How could the Book of the Law be lost, and was it really written by Moses?

The text says the book was found during repairs and calls it the book of the LORD's law given through Moses. After Manasseh's long idolatry, it is plausible that copies of the law were neglected, hidden or destroyed. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, identify the book with Deuteronomy or a form of it, because the reform's emphases, one place of worship, the high places destroyed, the covenant curses and a Passover at the central sanctuary, match that book closely.

Traditional interpreters take the attribution at face value: an ancient book of Moses, recovered after decades of neglect. Since the early nineteenth century many critical scholars have argued that Deuteronomy took its final form in the seventh century BC, drawing on older traditions or written to support the reform, and some see the discovery account as a way of giving it authority. Others propose a middle view, with ancient material from Moses edited over time. All readers agree on the text's claim that when the word was heard it demanded a response, and the king obeyed.
passages.asks: When Josiah heard God's words, he tore his clothes. Ask when God's word last troubled you enough to change something. And ask what parts of Scripture you have lost in your own house through neglect.
